lessons.title: The DataModel and finding things
lessons.summary: game, services, the instance tree, and the safe ways to find children.

sections.heading: Everything is a tree
sections.body:
Everything in a running Roblox game lives in one big tree of instances called the **DataModel**, and `game` is its root. Directly under `game` are the **services**: `Workspace` (the 3D world), `Players`, `ReplicatedStorage`, `ServerScriptService`, `Lighting` and many more. Everything else hangs below those.

Each instance has a `Name`, a `ClassName` saying what kind of thing it is, and a `Parent`, the instance it sits inside. Setting `Parent` moves an instance in the tree; setting it to `nil` takes it out of the game entirely.

sections.heading: Getting services
sections.body:
Get services with `game:GetService("Players")` rather than `game.Players`. GetService works even if a service hasn't been created yet, and keeps working if a service's name changes, so it's the standard at the top of every script. The Workspace has a shortcut, the global `workspace`.

The usual habit is to fetch the services a script needs into locals at the very top, named after the service, so every later line can use them.

example.caption: Services at the top of a script
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
print(#Players:GetPlayers(), "players online")
example.explain: Each service is fetched once and reused through its local.

sections.heading: Finding children
sections.body:
A dot, like `workspace.Pizzeria`, finds a child by name, but **errors** if it isn't there. `FindFirstChild("Pizzeria")` returns the child or `nil`, so you can check and react. Pass `true` as a second argument to search all descendants, not just direct children.

`WaitForChild("Pizzeria")` **yields** until the child exists, which matters wherever things load in over time, especially on the client. Give it a timeout as a second argument, like 5 seconds, and it returns `nil` instead of waiting forever. Without one, it warns in the Output after about five seconds but keeps waiting.

sections.heading: Lists and checks
sections.body:
`GetChildren()` returns an array of an instance's direct children, and `GetDescendants()` returns everything below it at any depth. Loop over them with the loops you already know.

`IsA("BasePart")` checks whether an instance is a certain class **or inherits from it**, so it's true for Parts, MeshParts and other part types. Comparing `ClassName` only matches the exact class. `FindFirstChildOfClass` and `FindFirstAncestor` round out the toolkit for searching up and down the tree.

When a search fails, print the full path of what you did find with `GetFullName()`. Seeing the real location usually reveals a typo or a part that sits one folder deeper than you thought.

key_points: `game` is the root of the DataModel, and services sit directly under it.
Use `game:GetService` to get services, once at the top of a script.
A dot errors on missing children, `FindFirstChild` returns `nil`, `WaitForChild` yields.
`IsA` checks a class and everything that inherits from it.
mistakes: Using a dot for something that might not exist yet.
Calling `WaitForChild` without a timeout on something that may never appear.
Checking `ClassName == "Part"` when any BasePart would do.
lessons.try_it: In a Script, print the name of every child of the Workspace, then every descendant that IsA BasePart. Try `FindFirstChild` with a name that doesn't exist and print the result.

quiz.question: What does `workspace:FindFirstChild("Ghost")` return if there's no child called Ghost?
quiz.explain: FindFirstChild returns nil when nothing matches, so you can check for it.

quiz.question: What does `part:IsA("BasePart")` return for a MeshPart?
quiz.explain: IsA includes parent classes, and MeshPart is a kind of BasePart.

quiz.question: Why prefer `game:GetService("Players")` to `game.Players`?
choices: It runs on the client only
It works even if the service hasn't been created yet
It creates a new Players service
quiz.explain: GetService finds or creates the service, so it's always safe.

lessons.title: Creating instances, attributes and tags
lessons.summary: Instance.new, Clone and Destroy, storing your own data with attributes, and grouping with tags.

sections.heading: Creating and destroying
sections.body:
`Instance.new("Part")` creates a brand new instance of any class. Set its properties, then set `Parent` **last**: once an instance is in the game, every property change has to be processed and replicated, so configuring it first is faster and avoids a flicker of half-made objects.

`Clone()` copies an instance and everything inside it, which is how you spawn things from a template stored in `ServerStorage`. `Destroy()` removes an instance for good, disconnects its events and locks its `Parent` so it can't come back.

example.caption: Building a part in code
example.code:
local crate = Instance.new("Part")
crate.Name = "Crate"
crate.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
crate.Anchored = true
crate.Parent = workspace
example.explain: Every property is set before the crate enters the world.

sections.heading: Attributes
sections.body:
**Attributes** are your own named values stored on any instance: `SetAttribute("Haunted", true)` and `GetAttribute("Haunted")`. They hold simple values like numbers, strings, booleans, `Vector3`s and `Color3`s, but not tables or instances. Setting one to `nil` removes it.

They show up in the Properties window, so you can set them in Studio too, and attributes set on the server **replicate** to clients automatically. That makes them a simple, powerful way to share state, like whether a lamp is on or what stage of the night it is.

In your pizza game, attributes like `TargetHouse` and `GameState` already do exactly this: the server sets them, and every client script can react.

sections.heading: Tags
sections.body:
A **tag** is a label you put on many instances so code can find them all, wherever they are in the tree. `instance:AddTag("Lamp")` adds one, `instance:HasTag("Lamp")` checks, and `CollectionService:GetTagged("Lamp")` returns every instance with that tag. You can add tags in Studio's Properties window as well.

Tags beat searching folders when similar objects are scattered around the map. One script can handle every tagged lamp in the game, however many you place.

sections.heading: Cleaning up
sections.body:
Anything you create, you're responsible for removing. Parts spawned for an effect, a customer at a door, a temporary marker: destroy them when they're finished, or the game slowly fills with leftovers that cost memory and performance.

For things that should simply disappear after a while, `Debris:AddItem(instance, seconds)` from the Debris service destroys it later without you needing to keep a timer. And keep your own references tidy: after destroying something, set any variable or table entry that pointed at it to `nil`.

key_points: `Instance.new` creates, `Clone` copies, `Destroy` removes for good.
Set properties first and `Parent` last.
Attributes store your own simple values on instances, and replicate from server to client.
Tags label many instances so `CollectionService:GetTagged` can find them.
mistakes: Using the second argument of `Instance.new` to set the parent before other properties.
Trying to store a table in an attribute.
Spawning things and never destroying them.
lessons.try_it: Create ten small anchored parts in a row with a loop, tag them all, give each a number attribute for its position in the row, then use `GetTagged` to destroy every part with an even number.

quiz.question: Why set `Parent` last when creating an instance?
choices: Parent can only be set once
Configuring it before it enters the game is faster and avoids flicker
quiz.explain: Changes made before parenting don't need to be processed and replicated one by one.

quiz.question: Which value can an attribute NOT hold?
quiz.explain: Attributes hold simple values. Tables and instances aren't allowed.

quiz.question: What does `CollectionService:GetTagged("Lamp")` return?
choices: An array of every instance tagged Lamp
quiz.explain: It returns all instances carrying that tag, wherever they are.

lessons.title: Vector3 and positions
lessons.summary: Positions and directions in 3D, distances with Magnitude, and directions with Unit.

sections.heading: Three numbers for a point
sections.body:
A `Vector3` holds three numbers: X and Z run along the ground, and Y goes **up**. You make one with `Vector3.new(x, y, z)` and read its parts with `.X`, `.Y` and `.Z`. Vector3s are values, like numbers: you can't change one in place, you make new ones.

The same type means two different things depending on use. A **position** is a point in the world. A **direction** or **offset** is a movement, like "3 studs up". Adding an offset to a position gives a new position.

sections.heading: Vector maths
sections.body:
Adding two Vector3s adds each part, and subtracting does the same. Multiplying by a number scales: doubling an offset makes it twice as long. The key move is subtraction: `target - origin` gives the offset that gets you from origin to target.

Handy constants include `Vector3.zero`, `Vector3.one` and `Vector3.yAxis` (straight up). `a:Lerp(b, 0.5)` gives the point halfway between two positions, and any fraction from 0 to 1 slides between them.

example.caption: Moving a point up
example.code:
local door = Vector3.new(10, 0, -4)
local above = door + Vector3.new(0, 3, 0)
print(above)
print(above - door)
example.explain: Prints the raised position, then the offset between them, 0, 3, 0.

sections.heading: Distance and direction
sections.body:
`.Magnitude` gives a vector's length. So the distance between two points is the magnitude of their difference: `(a - b).Magnitude`. That one expression answers questions like "is the player close to the door" and "which lamp is nearest".

`.Unit` gives a vector pointing the same way with length 1, a pure **direction**. Multiply a unit vector by a number to move exactly that far in that direction. Be careful: the unit of a zero-length vector is undefined, so check the distance isn't zero before using `.Unit` on it.

Comparing squared distances avoids a square root, but in Roblox `Magnitude` is fast enough that clarity wins. Write the obvious version first.

sections.heading: Circles and angles
sections.body:
Placing things around a circle uses the same maths as chapter 7's `math.cos` and `math.sin`. For an angle in radians, `math.cos(angle) * radius` gives the X offset and `math.sin(angle) * radius` gives the Z offset. Spreading `count` items evenly means angles of `math.pi * 2 * i / count`.

Roblox angles are in **radians**, where a full turn is `math.pi * 2`. `math.rad(degrees)` converts from degrees when that's easier to think in.

key_points: `Vector3.new(x, y, z)` with Y pointing up. Vector3s are values you replace, not change.
`target - origin` gives the offset from one point to another.
`(a - b).Magnitude` is the distance between two points. `.Unit` is a direction of length 1.
Cos and sin of an angle place points around a circle. Angles are in radians.
mistakes: Trying to set `position.X = 5`. Make a new Vector3 instead.
Passing degrees where radians are expected.
lessons.try_it: Place eight small parts evenly around a circle of radius 10, then print which one is closest to a point you choose, using Magnitude.

quiz.question: Which axis points up in Roblox?
quiz.explain: Y is up. X and Z run along the ground.

quiz.question: How do you get the distance between positions `a` and `b`?
quiz.explain: The difference is the offset between them, and its length is the distance.

quiz.question: What is the length of any vector's `.Unit`?
quiz.explain: Unit keeps the direction and makes the length exactly 1.

lessons.title: Parts and CFrames
lessons.summary: Part properties, colours and materials, and CFrame for position plus rotation.

sections.heading: Part properties
sections.body:
A Part's key properties: `Size` and `Position` (Vector3s), `Anchored` (true means physics never moves it), `CanCollide` (whether things bump into it), `Transparency` (0 is solid, 1 is invisible), `Color` (a `Color3`), and `Material`.

Colours come from `Color3.fromRGB(255, 200, 80)` with values from 0 to 255. Materials and many other choices are **Enums**, fixed lists of options: `Enum.Material.Neon` makes a part glow, and `Enum.Material.SmoothPlastic` is the plain default look. Studio autocompletes Enum names, so you rarely need to remember them.

Unanchored parts are simulated by physics: they fall, tumble and get pushed. Anchor anything that should stay put, like buildings and lamps.

sections.heading: CFrame: position plus rotation
sections.body:
A `Vector3` says where something is. A **CFrame** (coordinate frame) says where it is **and** which way it faces. Every part has a `CFrame` property, and setting it moves and rotates the part at once.

`CFrame.new(position)` makes one with no rotation. `CFrame.lookAt(position, target)` makes one at `position` facing `target`, perfect for turning a customer to face the player. A CFrame's `.Position` is its point, and `.LookVector` is a unit vector pointing out of its front.

example.caption: Facing the road
example.code:
local sign = Instance.new("Part")
sign.Anchored = true
sign.CFrame = CFrame.lookAt(Vector3.new(0, 4, 0), Vector3.new(0, 4, 20))
sign.Parent = workspace
print(sign.CFrame.LookVector)
example.explain: The sign stands at 0, 4, 0 facing along the Z axis, so its LookVector is 0, 0, 1.

sections.heading: Combining CFrames
sections.body:
Multiplying CFrames combines them: the right-hand one is applied **relative** to the left-hand one. `part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` is five studs in front of the part, whichever way it faces, because negative Z is "forward" in a CFrame's own space. Adding a Vector3 to a CFrame moves it in **world** space instead.

`CFrame.Angles(x, y, z)` makes a pure rotation in radians, so multiplying by `CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0)` turns something a quarter turn around the up axis.

sections.heading: Moving whole models
sections.body:
A Model groups parts. To move one, use `model:PivotTo(cframe)`, which moves every part together and keeps them in the same arrangement. `model:GetPivot()` returns where it is now. Setting one part's position would leave the rest of the model behind.

The same methods work on single parts too, so PivotTo is a good default whenever you move anything. Getting into the habit now saves you from a whole class of models that come apart when they move.

key_points: `Anchored`, `CanCollide`, `Transparency`, `Color` and `Material` control how a part behaves and looks.
Colours use `Color3.fromRGB`, and choices like materials use Enums.
A CFrame is position plus rotation. `CFrame.lookAt` faces a target.
Multiplying CFrames moves relative to the left one. Models move with `PivotTo`.
mistakes: Forgetting `Anchored`, so a part falls through the world or rolls away.
Moving one part of a model instead of pivoting the whole model.
lessons.try_it: Make a part that faces another part using `CFrame.lookAt`, then place a third part five studs in front of the first using CFrame multiplication. Change the colours and materials of all three.

quiz.question: What does `CFrame.lookAt(a, b)` give?
choices: The distance from a to b
A CFrame at a facing towards b
A CFrame at b facing a
The midpoint of a and b
quiz.explain: lookAt positions the frame at its first argument, facing the second.

quiz.question: `part.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -5)` is where?
choices: Five studs behind the world origin
Five studs in front of the part, whichever way it faces
quiz.explain: Multiplying applies the offset in the part's own space, where negative Z is forward.

quiz.question: How should you move a whole Model?
quiz.explain: PivotTo moves every part together, keeping the model's shape.

lessons.title: Events and connections
lessons.summary: Signals, Connect and Disconnect, the most useful events, and debouncing touches.

sections.heading: Signals
sections.body:
An **event** (or signal) is something an instance announces when it happens: a part being touched, a property changing, a child being added. You react by **connecting** a function: `signal:Connect(fn)`. Roblox calls `fn` every time the event fires, passing details as arguments, like the part that touched.

This is the main way Roblox code runs. Instead of loops constantly checking "has anything happened?", your functions are called exactly when something does.

The function you connect is usually a closure, capturing the instance it belongs to, which is exactly what chapter 8 prepared you for.

sections.heading: Connections
sections.body:
`Connect` returns a **connection**. Call `connection:Disconnect()` to stop listening. Destroying an instance disconnects its own events automatically, but connections to things that live on, like a player or a service, stay alive until you disconnect them, and keep everything they captured alive too. Long-running games that forget this slowly leak memory.

`signal:Once(fn)` connects for one firing only and disconnects itself. `signal:Wait()` yields until the event next fires and returns its arguments, handy in a script that waits for one moment.

example.caption: Listening, then stopping
example.code:
local connection = workspace.ChildAdded:Connect(function(child)
	print("New in the world:", child.Name)
end)
task.wait(10)
connection:Disconnect()
example.explain: Reports new children for ten seconds, then stops listening.

sections.heading: Events you'll use most
sections.body:
`instance:GetPropertyChangedSignal("Transparency")` fires when that property changes. `instance:GetAttributeChangedSignal("On")` fires when that attribute changes, which is how attribute-driven code reacts instantly. `ChildAdded`, `ChildRemoved` and `DescendantAdded` track the tree, and `Destroying` fires just before an instance is destroyed.

`BasePart.Touched` fires when something touches a part, passing the part that touched it. A **BindableEvent** is an event you own: call `:Fire(...)` on it and anything connected to its `Event` runs, letting scripts on the same side notify each other.

sections.heading: Debouncing
sections.body:
`Touched` fires a lot. A character walking onto a pad touches it with each foot, many times a second. If each touch gives a coin, one step pays out ten times. A **debounce** stops that: a flag or table that says "already handled, ignore for now".

For per-player effects, keep a table keyed by player: if the player is in the table, return early; otherwise add them, do the work, and remove them after a cooldown with `task.delay`. Most reward and damage code in Roblox games needs this pattern.

key_points: `signal:Connect(fn)` runs fn every time the event fires, with details as arguments.
Keep the returned connection and `Disconnect` it when you're done listening.
`GetAttributeChangedSignal` and `GetPropertyChangedSignal` react to specific changes.
Debounce events like Touched so one action isn't handled many times.
mistakes: Connecting the same handler again every time something happens, so it runs many times.
Never disconnecting connections to long-lived objects.
Rewarding every Touched event without a debounce.
lessons.try_it: Give a part a boolean attribute and connect to its attribute-changed signal so the part's colour changes whenever the attribute does. Toggle the attribute in Studio's Properties window during a playtest, then disconnect after five changes.

quiz.question: What does `Connect` return?
quiz.explain: Keeping the connection lets you stop listening later.

quiz.question: Which event fires when an attribute named `On` changes?
quiz.explain: Attributes have their own changed signal, separate from properties.

quiz.question: Why does a coin pad need a debounce?
choices: Touched fires many times for one step, so it would pay out repeatedly
Touched only works with a debounce
To save the coins to a DataStore
quiz.explain: Without it, every touch from every body part counts as a new pickup.
